body: きょう（8日）未明、愛知県で最大震度5強を観測する強い地震がありました。気象庁は、午前3時すぎに記者会見を行い、今後1週間程度は強い揺れを伴う地震に注意するよう呼びかけました。【写真で見る】気象庁会見　愛知県・知多市で最大震度5強の地震気象庁 地震火山部　海老田綾貴 課長「揺れの強かった地域では、落石・崖崩れなどの危険性が高まっていますので、今後の地震活動、あるいは降雨の状況に十分注意をお願いいたします」きょう（8日）午前1時4分ごろ、愛知県・知多市で最大震度5強を観測する強い地震がありました。震源地は静岡県西部で、震源の深さは41km、地震の規模を示すマグニチュードは暫定値で5.7となっています。この地震で、関東から四国地方の広い範囲で揺れを観測しています。気象庁によりますと、愛知県内で震度5強以上が観測されたのは、1997年3月16日に発生した愛知県東部を震源とするマグニチュード5.9の地震で、豊橋市向山で震度5強を観測して以来、およそ30年ぶりです。気象庁は揺れの強かった地域は落石や崖崩れの危険があるとしたうえで、1週間ほど、特に今後2～3日間は今回と同じ、震度5強程度の地震に注意するよう呼びかけています。また、今回の地震は、南海トラフ地震の想定震源域の中で発生しましたが、▼巨大地震を引き起こすプレート境界で起きた地震ではなくプレートの内部で起きた地震で、▼プレートの状態も目立った変化を示すものではないとしています。気象庁は、今後も地震活動や地殻変動を監視していくとしています。

title: あす都心11℃予想 12月下旬並み
body:
北日本を中心に強い寒気の流れ込みが続いています。9日(月)は雨の影響もあり、関東など12月下旬並みの寒さになる所もあるでしょう。10日(火)は北海道で真冬並みの寒気が流れ込み、雪の範囲が広がりそうです。雪道を運転する際は、冬用タイヤを装着するなど、対策をしてください。
今日8日(日)は冬型の気圧配置が緩みますが、10日(火)にかけてこの時期としては強い寒気の流れ込みが続くでしょう。今日8日(日)は昼頃まで山陰から北陸は雨、東北の日本海側は雨や雪が降りそうです。北海道の日本海側は断続的に雪が降り、朝のうちは暴風に警戒してください。明日9日(月)は低気圧の影響で、沖縄や九州から近畿、北陸は午後になると雨の範囲が広がり、東海は所々で雨が降るでしょう。関東甲信と東北は断続的に雨が降り、夜は東北の平地でも雪に変わる所がありそうです。北海道は昼頃から再び日本海側で雪が降り、ふぶく所もあるでしょう。10日(火)になると、北海道の上空1500メートル付近でマイナス12℃以下と真冬並みの寒気が流れ込み、雪の降り方が強まりそうです。平地でも雪が降る目安のマイナス6℃以下の寒気が東北まで流れ込み、東北は北部を中心に平地でも降るものは雪になるでしょう。北陸や関東甲信は、標高の高い山で雪の降る所がありそうです。
寒気の流れ込みによって、地上の気温も平年より低い所が増えるでしょう。明日9日(月)は雨の影響もあり、最高気温は東京都心と新潟で11℃、仙台で9℃と朝からあまり上がりません。東京都心は12月下旬並みの寒さになるでしょう。10日(火)は、晴れる所でも空気は冷たいままで、九州から東海では16℃から18℃くらいの所が多い見込みです。トレンチコートや厚手の上着が必要なくらいでしょう。札幌は日中でも1℃、朝晩は氷点下の冷え込みとなりそうです。寒さ対策を心がけてください。
雪道をノーマルタイヤで走行すると、タイヤが低温で固くなって吸着性が失われ、路面を摩擦で捉えることができなくなります。このため「滑る」「止まらない」「曲がらない」と、自動車が本来確保しなければならない動きが制御できなくなり、スリップ事故や渋滞の原因につながってしまいます。雪道を時速40kmで走った場合、ブレーキを踏んでからクルマが止まるまでの距離は、ノーマルタイヤでは冬用タイヤの約1.7倍にもなるという走行実験結果もあります。雪道でのノーマルタイヤは、とても危険ですので、冬用タイヤやチェーンを必ず装着するようにしてください。雪や雨が降ったあとの路面は凍結していることもあります。一見、路面に雪がないように見えても車の運転には十分な注意が必要です。

title: 互いに譲らず 冷え切った日中関係
body:
高市首相の台湾有事を巡る国会答弁から７日で１年。対立が長期化する日中関係の現状と課題を追う。【写真】写真で振り返る日中関係
「彼をペルソナ・ノン・グラータ（好ましくない人物）にすると伝えてきて」
答弁から約１週間後の昨年１１月中旬、首相は木原官房長官や外務省幹部らを集めた会議でこう語った。首相答弁に反発し、ＳＮＳ上で「その汚い首は斬ってやるしかない」と投稿した中国の薛剣（シュエジエン）・駐大阪総領事について、早期に帰任させなければ国外退去にすると中国側に伝えるよう指示したものだ。
ペルソナ・ノン・グラータは国際法で認められた措置で、通告すれば外交官を一方的に追放できる。任国の首脳の殺害を予告するかのような発言は、外交儀礼に著しくもとるもので、与党からは追放を求める声が相次いでいた。他方、相手国からは強い反発が予想され、外交では「禁断のカード」とされてきた。
首相が念頭に置いたのは、支持基盤の保守層を中心とする世論の声だ。首相の対中姿勢は世論から肯定的に受け止められ、読売新聞の同１１月下旬の世論調査でも６割弱が支持し、首相の判断を支えていた。
目算は狂う。指示を受けた金井正彰外務省アジア大洋州局長が中国外務省の劉勁松（リウジンソン）アジア局長（当時）と北京で会談し、追放検討を伝えると、劉氏は、中国駐在の総領事を名指しし、「１人を追放すれば、こちらは２人だ」と予告した。
日本側は、薛氏を追放した場合、総領事１人が中国から追放を受け、「痛み分け」で手打ちにするシナリオを想定した。だが、中国が示したのは「倍返し」だ。報告を受けた首相は追放の見送りを決めた。報復の連鎖がさらなる関係悪化につながることを懸念したためで、「対話の余地を残すためのギリギリの判断」（日本政府関係者）だった。
事の発端となった答弁は、台湾有事で集団的自衛権が行使できるかどうかを野党議員に衆院予算委員会で詰められた際に飛び出した。首相は、台湾周辺で活動する米軍に中国が武力を行使すれば「どう考えても存立危機事態になり得る」と答え、集団的自衛権行使の対象との認識を示した。

title: ポーランドで銃乱射事件 6人死亡
body: 【ベルリン共同】ポーランド南部クラクフで7日、男が中心部の広場に車で突入して車内から通行人らに向かって無差別に銃を乱射し、6人が死亡、警察官2人を含む15人が負傷した。ポーランドのメディアが伝えた。男は警察官と撃ち合いになって負傷し、拘束後に病院に搬送された。報道によると、男は24歳のポーランド人。軍服のような服装だったが軍歴はなく、車内に多数の銃器や弾薬が残されていた。動機は判明していない。極右思想に染まっていたとの情報もある。トゥスク首相は「悲劇的な銃撃事件だ」とX（旧ツイッター）に投稿。記者会見で男の自宅から家族とみられる男女3人が死亡しているのが見つかったと明らかにした。地元メディアは、多くの警察官や救急隊員が活動し、騒然とする広場周辺の様子を報じた。クラクフはポーランド南部オシフィエンチムにあるナチス・ドイツのアウシュビッツ強制収容所跡を訪れる際の拠点となる街。銃撃事件の現場は聖マリア教会などで知られる中央市場広場で、観光客が多く訪れる旧市街にある。

title: 米中間選挙 共和党大敗の舞台裏
body: 中間選挙で歴史的な大敗を喫したトランプ大統領率いる共和党。これまで「共和党の牙城」と言われてきたテキサス州では民主党の上院議員候補が当選するなど、大きな地殻変動が起きた。選挙戦の舞台裏を取材すると深い分断を目の当たりにした一方で、アメリカ民主主義のしなやかさも見えてきた。【写真を見る】アメリカ中間選挙で共和党大敗の舞台裏　“異変”は選挙前から【報道特集】■トランプ氏「自分が候補者なら勝っていた」アメリカ中間選挙で共和党が大敗中間選挙の投票日、報道特集が取材に入ったのは激戦州テキサス。共和党の牙城とされてきたが、民主党の上院議員候補、タラリコ氏の優勢が伝えられていた。村瀬健介キャスター「タラリコ候補の当選確実が出ました。会場総立ち、喜びで包まれています。民主党にとっての大金星です。大きな大きな1議席を取りました」――おめでとうございます。民主党支持者「ありがとう。なんてこと。すごい、信じられない。素晴らしい、最高です。よくやったテキサス」喜びの渦は別の会場でも。民主党支持者「タラリコ!タラリコ!」「トランプは退陣しろ」上院選で勝利　民主党・タラリコ氏「我々はテキサスを取り戻した」テキサスの上院選挙で、38年ぶりに民主党が議席を獲得した。同じ激戦州のミシガンでも。上院選で勝利　民主党・エルサイード氏「ミシガンの皆さん、やりました」民主党のエルサイード候補が勝利を宣言。イスラム教徒として初めての上院議員が誕生する。上院100議席のうち35議席と下院の全議席が改選されたが、上院、下院ともに民主党が過半数を獲得した。投票から一夜明け、「選挙戦に悔いはない」とした上で、トランプ大統領は…トランプ大統領「もし自分が候補者だったら勝っていたんだ。どの集会にも何千もの人がいたのに、その熱狂を候補者たちが伝えられなかった」“敗北は候補者の責任だ”と言わんばかりだ。共和党が大敗した選挙戦の裏側でいったい何が起きていたのか。■強固な地盤のはずも…カンザス州で94年ぶりに民主党の上院議員が誕生アメリカ中間選挙、共和党大敗の予兆は強固な地盤でも。

title: 米首席補佐官交代 強硬路線進むか
body: アメリカのトランプ大統領はワイルズ大統領首席補佐官を交代させ、保守強硬派のミラー次席補佐官を後任にすることを決めました。中継です。【画像で見る】激戦州を争った候補たち トランプ政権で中間選挙“大敗”中間選挙の直後には「民主党と協力の余地がある」と話していたトランプ大統領ですが、新たに首席補佐官に起用するのは民主党との対決姿勢を前面に打ち出す保守強硬派でした。アメリカ　トランプ大統領「ワイルズ氏はとても良い仕事、素晴らしい仕事をしてくれた。だが、私には変化が必要だった。ミラー氏は素晴らしい。我々は動き出さないといけない」トランプ大統領は6日、ワイルズ大統領首席補佐官を交代させ、ミラー次席補佐官を後任にすると発表しました。ミラー氏はトランプ政権の強硬な不法移民対策を主導し、大規模な強制送還などを進めてきた人物です。ミラー氏が政権の要の首席補佐官となることで、今後、政策は一段と強硬路線に傾き、来年1月から議会で多数派となる民主党との対立が激しくなることが予想されます。また、退任するワイルズ氏はトランプ氏に苦言を呈することもできる「猛獣使い」として知られてきましたが、ミラー氏はトランプ氏と長く行動を共にしてきた忠実な側近で、衝動的に動くことも少なくないトランプ氏への「歯止め」はますます弱まる見通しです。

title: 露 ウのエネ施設に大規模攻撃
body: ロシア軍がウクライナのエネルギー施設を狙った大規模な攻撃を行い、ゼレンスキー大統領は首都キーウの電気や暖房の供給に深刻な問題が出ていると明らかにしました。【写真で見る】ロシア軍に攻撃され炎上する住宅　ウクライナのエネルギー施設を狙った大規模な攻撃ウクライナのゼレンスキー大統領は7日、ロシア軍が172機のドローンと36発の弾道ミサイルを使い、首都キーウや周辺地域を攻撃したと明らかにしました。ウクライナ空軍によりますと、このうちウクライナ側が迎撃できた弾道ミサイルはわずか4発だったということです。ゼレンスキー氏は、原子力発電所から首都キーウなどに電力を送る施設が損傷したと明らかにしたうえで、「キーウでは電気や水道、暖房の供給に深刻な問題が出ている」と懸念を示しました。また、現地メディアは、キーウの重要な交通インフラである北部の橋が損傷したほか、全土でこれまでに2人が死亡し、30人以上がけがをしたと伝えています。ロシア軍は冬を前に、ウクライナの市民生活を脅かすエネルギー施設への攻撃を強めています。ロシアとウクライナは、アメリカが仲介する和平に向けた3か国協議を10日からUAE=アラブ首長国連邦の首都アブダビで再開する予定です。

title: 露 JT法人3社を一時管理下に追加
body: ロシアのプーチン大統領は、JT=日本たばこ産業の現地法人3社を新たにロシア企業の一時管理下に置く大統領令に署名しました。対象は合わせて7社となり、JTグループは現地での製造から販売に至る事業の経営権を事実上失う見通しです。6日付の大統領令で新たに対象となったのは、JTグループの「JTIロシア」など販売や経営管理などを担う3社です。プーチン大統領は5日にも、たばこの製造を担う4社をロシア企業の一時管理下に置く大統領令に署名していて、対象は合わせて7社となりました。ロシアメディアによりますと、今回対象となった3社は、輸入や経営管理、持ち株会社としての機能などを担っています。これにより、JTグループは現地の工場だけでなく、販売や経営管理を担う企業についても経営の主導権を失うことになります。日本政府は5日の措置を受けてロシア側に抗議し、撤回を求めていましたが、さらに対象が拡大した形です。一方、ロシア外務省の幹部は6日に公開されたインタビューで、「非友好国」の資産を一時管理下に置く措置について、「外国による露骨な敵対的行為への対抗措置だ」と主張しています。

title: 東海道新幹線 地震で最大60分遅れ
body:
８日午前１時すぎ、静岡県西部を震源とした強い地震がありました。県内では浜松市浜名区で最大震度５弱を観測しています。気象庁によりますと、８日午前１時４分ごろ、静岡県西部を震源とする強い地震がありました。震源の深さはおよそ４１キロ、地震の規模を示すマグニチュードは５・７と推定されます。県内では浜松市浜名区で震度５弱、浜松市中央区や天竜区、島田市、磐田市などで震度４を観測しています。被害の情報です。消防によりますと、掛川市で３０代の女性が右肩を脱臼し病院に搬送されました。女性は軽傷です。また森町では９０代の女性がベッドから転落して、右肩を負傷し病院に搬送されました。磐田市では５０代の女性と８０代の女性が地震後、動悸やめまいなどを訴え救急搬送されています。
交通にも影響が出ています。ＪＲ東海によりますと、県内では地震の影響で寝台特急「サンライズ出雲」の下り線が、東海道線の舞阪駅と高塚駅で停車していましたが、午前３時半すぎに動き始めました。乗客およそ２９０人に体調不良やけがはないということです。また東海道新幹線は地震の影響により、静岡駅から岐阜羽島駅の間で速度を落として運転を行うため、上下列車に最大６０分程度の遅れが見込まれるとしています。このほか、中部電力によりますと、御前崎市にある浜岡原発に地震の影響は確認されていないということです。静岡県庁は地震発生直後から警戒体制を敷き、市や町から上がってきた被害などの状況をまとめています。気象庁は、午前３時すぎに会見を開き、揺れの強かった地域では今後１週間程度最大震度５強程度の地震に注意するよう呼び掛けています。

title: テスラ サイバートラック生産縮小
body: 【ニューヨーク時事】米電気自動車大手テスラのイーロン・マスク最高経営責任者（CEO）は6日、SNSのXへの投稿で、ピックアップトラック「サイバートラック」の南部テキサス州での生産を2027年半ばに縮小すると発表した。【動画】テスラのピックアップトラック「サイバートラック」外装にステンレスを使い、角張ったデザインで、発売当初から賛否両論を巻き起こしてきたが、市場に浸透できなかった。マスク氏は、サイバートラックの生産縮小について、自動運転タクシー車両「サイバーキャブ」の増産を進める狙いだと説明。サイバートラックの担当技術者はXで、「サイバートラックは素晴らしい技術開発基盤となった。（その成果は）サイバーキャブを通じて生き続ける」と投稿した。

title: スーパーの衣料品売れない? 今後
body:
スーパーの衣料品売り場は、転換期を迎えています。
日本チェーンストア協会の加盟企業では、衣料品売上高が2015年の約1兆1,920億円から2025年の約5,975億円へ、10年でほぼ半減。売上構成比も9.1％から4.6％に縮小しました。
サミットは9月、「コルモピア」21店舗の事業を「しまむら」に譲渡すると発表。11月4日の決算会見で、仕入れ難を説明しました。翌5日にはイオンが、靴専門店「ASBee」などを展開するジーフットとの合併基本合意を発表しました。
スーパーの服売り場は、これからどう変わるのでしょうか。
相次ぐスーパー再編 「飛び地出店」の狙いとは【NIKKEI NEWS NEXT】
サミット／コルモピア事業の譲渡、服部社長「去年から仕入れが厳しくなってきていた」出典：流通ニュース　2026/11/4(水)
イオン、「ASBee」のジーフットとイオンリテール合併　経営を効率化出典：日本経済新聞　2026/11/5(木)
２０２５年暦年（１月～１２月度）チェーンストア販売概況について出典：日本チェーンストア協会　2026/1/22(木)
かつてスーパーは、食品と一緒に家族の肌着や普段着、靴まで買える場所でした。
しかし、衣料品専門店やネット通販が選択肢を広げる中、スーパーが幅広い服を自前で仕入れ、売り続けることは難しくなっています。実際、サミットはコルモピアの譲渡について、店舗数や仕入れ力の限界を説明しています。
その変化に大きな影響を与えた存在の一つが「ユニクロ」でしょう。国内ユニクロ事業の売上収益は2015年8月期の7,801億円から2025年8月期には1兆260億円へ、約32％増加しました。今や国内アパレル市場の約10%を占めています。スーパーからユニクロ、しまむらなどの低価格帯のアパレルやEC、セカストなどの古着、そしてここにきてファミマなどのコンビニも注目を集めています。流出の規模を正確に把握することは難しいですが、衣料品を購入する場所が変わってきました。
恐らく、今後のスーパーの衣料品売り場は肌着や靴下、ヒットアイテムなど「食品の買い物ついでに買いたい服」は残しつつ、専門店に任せる店と、そのノウハウを自社の売り場に取り込む店に分かれるでしょう。サミットは前者、イオンは後者です。
皆さんはスーパーで衣料品を購入する機会は減りましたか？

title: 購買力高い大学生 なぜ存在する
body: ■要旨・日本の大学生は生活費負担がなく会社員の小遣い以上の購買力を保持。・生活費の有無で自由に使えるお金に大きな格差が生じる構造である。・就職後に使えるお金が減る逆転現象が若者の労働観に影響を与える。■はじめに筆者はこれまで、若者の消費行動を論じるなかで、繰り返し「若者はお金がない」という問題を取り上げてきた。所得が十分に高くないことや、物価上昇によって自由に使えるお金が限られていること、学生であれば親世代の家計事情によって仕送りや小遣いにも制約が生じることなどである。若者が消費に慎重になったり、欲しいものを諦めたりする背景には、こうした経済的な事情があると考えてきた。しかし、その一方で、明らかに羽振りのよい若者がいることも事実である。700円前後のフラペチーノをためらいなく注文したり、コンビニで数千円分の商品を購入したり、ラーメン一杯に2,000円を惜しげもなく支払ったりする若者の姿である。これらは高級店での特別な消費ではなく、私たち自身も日常的に利用する店で見かける光景である。だからこそ、自分なら価格を気にしたり、購入をためらったりするような金額を、彼らがさほど気にすることなく支払っているように映る。自分と同じ生活圏で目にする消費だからこそ、彼らの金銭的な余裕がより身近に、そして鮮明に感じられるのである。では、若者は本当にお金がないのだろうか。■サラリーマンより小遣いを持っている大学生ここで考えたいのが、本人の所得が少ないことと、自由に使えるお金が少ないことは、必ずしも同じではないという点である。例えば、大学生であっても、親の扶養の範囲を意識しながらアルバイトで月10万円程度を稼ぐことは十分に可能である。なかには、アルバイトをしながら親から小遣いを受け取っている学生もいるだろう。さらに、親の扶養から外れることや、自分で税金や社会保険料を負担することをいとわなければ、働く時間を増やして、より多くの収入を得ることも可能である。

title: What we know so far after Krakow gun attack
summary: Six people were killed in a random shooting in the city's main square, and three bodies were later found at his home.
body:
At least six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland.
Three bodies were found at his home when it was searched by police. Here's everything we know so far.
The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city.
Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car".
Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard.
A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured.
People run for shelter as gunshots heard in Krakow
Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said.
The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested.
Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times.
The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself.
Moment police officer appears to shoot Krakow suspect
Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor.
City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues.
The suspect's car, found at the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, was checked for possible explosive devices, police said, but none were found. Residents of nearby buildings had been evacuated while the operation was under way.
Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed, including a British national. Three victims are Polish and two have not been identified.
Sixteen people, including five foreigners and the attacker, were taken to hospital. Among those being treated are two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker. The interior ministry later said they were from Britain, Austria, Russia, Germany and Portugal.
Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk later named the injured officers as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur Morański.
Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack.
One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added.
Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims.
Police have identified the attacker as a 25-year-old Polish man but have not confirmed his name.
The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities have confirmed the attacker was not a soldier.
"Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added.
Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home.
A minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details.
His home is being searched with support from counter-terrorism police.
The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination.
Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started.
Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down.
"A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises."
Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend.
She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice".
Moment shooting heard in Krakow square
After travelling to Krakow, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said : "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow."
Krakow Mayor Łukasz Gibała has signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, 11 November.
US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack".
The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".

title: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
summary: Neither PM Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor that of his rival secured a majority in last week's election.
body:
Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government.
Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election.
Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension.
"Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X.
No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions.
Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48.
Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters.
That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government.
Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government.
A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision.
Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said.
The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats.
The election results had implied threepossible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties.
Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached.
He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult.
There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two.
During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled".
In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate.

title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
summary: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.
body:
New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addressed supporters in Auckland as votes were being counted
The electoral commission was not due to announce the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Hipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaking to supporters
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of renewing strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities.
body:
The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme.
The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details.
President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been"completely and totally obliterated" following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel.
Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon.
Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders.
The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies.
As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams.
Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil.
Major construction ongoing near Iran missile bases, satellite images suggest
A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel".
It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges".
Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher.
There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so.
In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said.
The president hasrepeatedly threatenedto bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions.
However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict.
On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military.
"We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said.
Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed.
Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions.
The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

title: Houthis say at least 25 killed in Saudi air strike
summary: Saudi Arabia, which leads a coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen, has not commented.
body:
Children were among the injured people seen being carried into a nearby hospital
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

title: Labubu hype seemed unstoppable, now the fluffy monster mania is dying
summary: Parent company Pop Mart's revenue has fallen as appetite for the quirky collectible monsters wanes.
body:
Ensito, with his custom-made Labubu teeth, posing with a new doll in his collection
For years, Labubu dolls seemed unstoppable.
Collectors young and old energetically snapped up "blind boxes" - sealed, mystery packages containing the quirky monsters - often paying $15 (£11) or more.
Those unable to get the characters they wanted were often prepared to pay much more on the resale market.
The hype around the creatures convinced a mega-fan from North Carolina, who goes by the name Ensito, to leave his tech job in 2024 to create Labubu content full-time, travelling as far as Italy and Spain to seek out the latest releases.
Ensito has spent more than $50,000 (£37,000) to build his collection of more than 400 Labubus, a figure he tells the BBC he's "embarrassed to say".
He even had a row of custom Labubu-like jagged teeth made by a dentist to wear at events.
But in recent months, Ensito's once-viral posts about the furry monsters have struggled. "Those videos used to be able to hit 10,000 really quickly but I'm struggling to do that now."
Ensito's focus has shifted to other trends like Hello Kitty and squishies.
It's a sign that the craze whichmade parent company Pop Mart worth more than US toy giants Hasbro and Mattel put togethermay be running out of steam. Analysts believe the Beijing-based brand is struggling to capture excitement beyond a single viral moment.
Pop Mart recently reported that global sales in the three months to the end of September had fallen by as much as 50% on the previous year.
The drop was particularly steep outside mainland China, with US revenue down by at least 70%.
Pop Mart didn't invent blind boxes but its dolls certainly helped to popularise them around the world.
The sales tactic made collecting feel "nostalgic", evoking the feeling of opening gifts as a child, says marketing professional Katelynn Carlson, who discovered Labubus through social media and now owns 36 of them.
One of her first Labubus was a rare doll, making the experience "even more exciting", she adds.
Labubu, which launched in 2019, has beenPop Mart's most successful line of toys. The monsters becamefashion statementsand were sported by celebrities including Kim Kardashian and Blackpink's Lisa.
They regularly attracted long queues and became so popular that Pop Mart had totemporarily pull the toys from its UK shopsafter reports of customers fighting over them. One fan paid more than$150,000 for a human-sized Labubu.
A key part of the allure was howdifficult some Labubu dolls were to find, with fans repeatedly buying blind boxes to get the version they wanted, says National University of Singapore marketing lecturer Samer El Hajjar.
Katelynn Carlson believes blind boxes were an exciting feature of the Labubu craze
Pop Mart now has 500 shops in more than 30 countries and 2,000 vending machines worldwide. The firm, which listed in Hong Kong in 2020, is worth nearly $24bn and remains one of the world's most valuable toymakers, despite its shares having fallen by more than 50% from last year's peak.
Investors worry its global success was just a viral moment rather than sustainable growth driven by long-term customer loyalty, El Hajjar says.
For Ensito, it is clear the dolls' exclusivity helped fuel the craze.
"Now it doesn't feel that way. I walk into a Pop Mart and there's a whole series of Labubus sitting there," he says.
Ashley Dudarenok of China research firm ChoZan says that sense of exclusivity faded as Pop Mart ramped up production to meet demand.
Pop Mart declined to comment on share price moves and did not respond to questions about falling sales.
As the Labubu mania cools, some of its rivals have become more popular.
Blind box collectables like Sonny Angels - tiny, unclothed cherub-like dolls - and miniature glow-in-the-dark Smiski figurines have been flying off shelves. And you can now find My Little Pony and KPop Demon Hunters in blind boxes too.
Miniso, founded in the southern Chinese city of Guangzhou, sells a range of blind-boxed Disney and Marvel characters in more than 8,000 shops globally.
"Consumers aren't particularly concerned about where the brand comes from," Miniso executive Vincent Huangsaid earlier this year. "They're more focused on the shopping experience - the designs, value for money, and enjoyment."
Pop Mart faces competition from retailers like Miniso
Experts say one of Pop Mart's biggest challenges is creating enduring characters.
That's an area where Hello Kitty brand Sanrio, which posted record earnings in the year to March, has a clear advantage, analyst Boustani suggests.
Pop Mart has invested heavily in ways to grow its brand, including setting up a theme park in Beijing andannouncing a Labubu film- following in the footsteps of franchising giants like Disney or Lego, some experts believe.
But unlike Disney, which sells a story before it sells a toy, Pop Mart is working in reverse, says Dudarenok. "The real test for next year is whether Pop Mart can make people love a character without a celebrity holding it."
Glow-in-the-dark Smiskis are emerging as a competitor to Labubus
After spending huge sums on the monsters, collector Ensito says he is now questioning how much time and money people invest in collections each time a new trend comes along. "There's always going to be a trend every year. There's always gonna be something that's gonna be really popular."
Melbourne-based content creator Lawrence Yu says that after two years of chasing Labubus, he's likely to be "more selective" before adding to his roughly 50 dolls.
His Labubu shopping and unboxing clips once drew up to a million views but the frenzy has faded and Yu rarely makes videos about them now. "I definitely think the trend has slowed down... People go crazy and then it fizzles."
Clara Barbero from Canada believes Labubus are a "dead trend" but is still keeping an eye out for interesting releases.
"I’m curating my collection more and only buying what I see myself liking for the next few years, and not just buying the newest series that’s out."
Lawrence Yu says he has spent about $1,400 on Labubu dolls
But the fluffy monsters still have truly devoted fans.
Hedy Khaled from Liverpool says although the hype around the dolls is cooling, she is just as attached to her collection of 70 Pop Mart figurines.
There's a distinction between those who chase trends and "real fans", she argues, so falling sales do not necessarily mean Labubus have lost their appeal.
For Carlson says it is the happiness the dolls bring, not the viral trend, that keeps her collecting. She still gets excited about new Pop Mart releases, like its recent cat-themed Labubu series, which has become one of her favourites.
"I think there's something special about embracing our inner child and enjoying things simply because they make us happy."

title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have recovered slightly from an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index closed in positive territory following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.
Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.
However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.
On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.
But the Nasdaq Composite bounced back slightly on Friday,ending the day up 1.1%,partlyreversing some of its 5.5% fall.
The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies,closed up 0.3%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Averagewas flat through the day before ending slightly down 0.4%.
Companies that lost hundreds of billions in market value recovered some ground on Friday, including Nvidia, SpaceX and Tesla.
However, stock markets in Asia and Europe fared worse.
The Kospi in South Korea closed down 6% on Friday, with shares in chipmaker SK Hynix plunging more than 10%. European markets also fell, with the main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ending the day down.
In the UK, the FTSE 100, which tracks the largest companies on the London Stock Exchange, declined 1.01%.
In addition to the recent market volatility, UK traders were also digesting the latest Bank of England decision to raise interest rates and the signal that another rate rise could be on the cards to curb rising prices.
The market fluctuations also come after the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections.
A number of Democrats campaigned for new rules and regulations for artificial intelligence (AI) and data centres, and the party has since won control of both houses of congress as well as key contests in states that have been part of the AI data centre race.
US President Donald Trump on Friday reiterated his supported for what he calls "super intelligence", saying only "foolish leadership" would "say no to the riches they bring".
However, there have also been concerns over whether the enormous amounts of money being spent on AI will pay off.
Russ Shaw, founder of global tech advocacy firm Tech London Advocates, said the election result was sending a message that a rethink was needed on AI.
"The incoming Congress is going to really focus on AI in a very dramatic way," he told the BBC's Business Today.
"I'm a big fan of AI, but I'm watching what these companies are doing, and they're not communicating effectively at all, particularly in the US, about what the benefits of AI are all about."
Pierre Baqué, chief executive of AI platform Neural Concept, said the share movements were a "necessary market correction" that reflected a legitimate concern about the amount of money being poured into AI infrastructure.
"The industry must move beyond unchecked infrastructure investment and demonstrate greater financial discipline," he said.
"We are entering a critical transition phase, a market purgatory where raw tech must prove its widespread economic value."
Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said it had been a brutal week for markets, and the key question was whether the jump in the S&P 500 and Nasdaq would be sustained.
"Once investors have had the weekend to catch their breath, next week could give a clearer indication of whether the tech trade is going down the pan or fighting back."
Could the US midterms put a pin in the AI bubble?
Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
As well as the fallout of the midterms and the plunge in artificial intelligence stocks, US traders will also be digesting the latest jobs figures.
And those numbers were better than expected: US employers added 165,000 new jobs in October, well above the average monthly increase and more than double what analysts had expected.
Overall the unemployment rate, which counts the number of people who are out of work but actively looking for a job, eased slightly to 4.1%from 4.2% in September.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) said the unemployment rate has remained in the narrow range of 4.1% to 4.3% since March.
Neil Birrell, chief investment officer at investment firm Premier Miton, said while the jobs figures may feel like second billing to the market movements they were still important.
"The US economy is running hard which may mean the risks the markets are worrying about at the moment are not such a risk to the real economy as is being feared," he said.

title: Why the US midterms sparked an AI stock selloff
summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but  concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
body:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?
That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.
The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.
It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's midterm elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.
A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.
Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have concerned investors. But worries about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.
The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.
Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and  networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.
The boom continued into this year. Investments in AI are expected to reach $1trillion in 2026 alone according to research by Goldman Sachs. The sector has scooped up so much available cash that other industries have seen their own borrowing costs increase as a result.
But investors want returns, and in recent months concerns have been growing about whether the AI boom can produce the expected riches.
Those worries have emerged at a time when public comments from AI researchers casting doubt over the safety of artificial intelligence - even suggesting it could represent an existential threat to humanity - have been grabbing headlines and fuelling speculation that a clampdown could lie ahead.
US tech stocks edge back up after AI slowdown fears sent value of firms plummeting
How does it affect me if share prices fall?
These firms you've never heard of are feeding fears the AI bubble could burst
While the Trump administration has been all-in on AI, or "super intelligence" as the president likes to call it, many leading Democrats tapped into grassroots concerns about the expansion of data centres and their impact on local communities.
These were largely focused on the facilities' high consumption of water and electricity, which many feared would push up their household bills – as well as the noise, use of land, and general disruption associated with them.
A Gallup poll published in May showed 71% of Americans would oppose the building of a data centre in their community. The figure for a nuclear power station was 53%.
James Talarico, who won the Senate race in once staunchly Republican Texas, was one of those to respond to this scepticism.
"While we want to protect America's leadership in artificial intelligence, we are still grappling with how it will affect everything from how we work to how our children learn," he said.
"We must protect Americans and establish clear, consistent laws for businesses."
With control of both houses of Congress, Democrats are now expected to challenge the president's technology agenda more vigorously, while introducing legislation which could curb the expansion of the industry.
Texas' Democratic governor-elect Gina Hinojosa campaigned against data centres, pledging a moratorium on the construction of new facilities.
Hinojosa's win could present opposition to tech multi-billionaire Elon Musk, who has moved large parts of SpaceX and Tesla's operations to the state, for years a Republican stronghold.
The Tesla boss had spent nearly $450m to back Republican campaigns in the midterms.
As the co-founder of the British-based technology firm Arm Holdings, Tudor Brown, points out, "stock values are based on future earnings not present earnings". If the rewards are not likely to be as great as expected, some investors will choose to sell up.
The falls seen on stock markets over the past 24 hours would appear to have been triggered by the midterm results. But concerns that tech firms have become overvalued were being expressed long before the elections.
The question now is whether this is simply the removal of froth from an over-exuberant market, or a sign that the AI rush is a bubble about to burst, with much wider consequences.
Nandini Roy Choudhury of Future Market Insights thinks investors will assess whether the political shift could result in restrictions on data centre construction, energy consumption and the deployment of AI technology.
She adds there is unlikely to be an immediate widespread recovery in tech stocks as traders are likely to be more selective, favouring firms with stronger balance sheets.
Brown thinks the impact will be limited. Share valuations, he thinks, were inflated by expectations of "almost infinite AI growth", which have been followed by "a bit of a panic".
"There is a natural floor to this", he says. "After that it will reflect I think that actually there's still a lot of money being made in these companies".

title: How does it affect me if share prices fall?
summary: Changes in the FTSE 100 and other indexes are not just for financial experts, they can affect our lives.
body:
Major tech firms have seen their stock values fall after a sell-off by investors following the US midterm elections.
The fall in the value of their shares across the world has been blamed on an expectation of a slowdown in AI development, although it comes after sharp rises over recent years.
As companies grow, they may issue shares. Many of the largest companies in the UK have shares which are bought and sold on the London Stock Exchange.
Their collective performance is often quoted amid a blizzard of numbers that may feel confusing and irrelevant.
Booms or falls in the stock market make the news, but rarely does anyone mention the FTSE 100 during a coffee with friends.
Yet, there are good reasons why this performance affects your life and finances.
Many people's initial reaction to "the markets" is that they are not directly affected, because they do not invest money.
Yet there are millions of people with a pension - either private or through work - who will see their savings (in what is known as a defined contribution pension) invested by pension schemes. The value of their savings pot is influenced by the performance of these investments.
Pension savers mostly let experts choose where to invest this money to help it grow. Widespread falls in share prices are likely to be bad news for pension savers.
Hundreds of billions of pounds are held in defined contribution pensions at the moment.
So big rises or falls can affect your pension, but the advice is to remember that pension savings, like any investments, are usually a long-term bet.
Experts say that investors have always had to ride economic shocks. Investments, by definition, require a long-term outlook and strategy. So, they are urging people not to panic in such circumstances or make knee-jerk decisions.
Some people have a pension which promises a specific value, depending on their salary. Others have no pension at all.
Millions of people have been automatically enrolled into a pension and may have not really noticed. Those schemes see employers divert wages into a pension and contribute some money themselves. The government adds a little in tax relief.
In every case, the value of these pension savings is affected by investment performance. So "the markets" matter - maybe not as much as everyday wages, but for future pensions.
Timing is more critical for those at retirement age, as this may be when a retiree uses their pension pot to buy a retirement income, or annuity. The bigger the pot, the more income they will get in retirement.
As you approach retirement age, pension pots tend to be moved to less risky investments, such as government bonds. When stock markets fall, these bonds can do better.
Anyone who has a pension pot invested and is taking an income from it will again see their investment go up and down with the stock markets.
That could mean getting less than you expected if you cash in too much after stock markets have fallen, making it important to plan how to make up any of this shortfall, experts say.
However, higher interest rates tend to mean better rates offered on annuities, and there is a chance of more rate rises in the UK by the Bank of England.
If share prices fall for an extended period then that could have an effect on jobs.
That's because investors in the company expect a return on that investment.
When it falls for a while, then they would expect the business to address issues, for example by cutting costs, and therefore jobs.
There is a huge element of the unknown here though. Companies have to consider lots of factors when making decisions on investment and employment.
In purely investment terms, lower share prices can offer an opportunity to buy, in the hope that over the long term, they recover and rise. Many people will do this initially through a stocks and shares Individual Savings Account (Isa).
However, it is worth noting that the sell-off in tech stocks in particular came after big rises, so long-term investors are still likely to have seen gains.
Experts and regulators are at pains to point out that investments can go down as well as up, and urge people not to put everything into one investment, but to diversify.
Some people invest money in what are known as tracker funds. These go up and down in line with the performance of a certain index, such as the FTSE 100.
So if the index falls, so does the value of their investments and vice versa. One advantage of these funds is that they often cost relatively little to sign up to.
Yes, and millions of people do, but experts stress that a long-term strategy is required to ride out short-term falls. It is also important to ensure cash savings are held too, so unexpected expenses - like the need for a replacement boiler - can be covered.
The government is keen to get people in the UK to invest more, partly because it says that will help UK economic growth and partly because it is much more popular among individuals in the US and some parts of Europe.
It backed an advertising campaign to encourage people to invest, funded by some of the UK's biggest financial services firms.
But the choice of "Savvy the Squirrel" to front the campaign has raised some eyebrows. Some question whether the push could get anywhere close to the success of the Tell Sid adverts of the 1980s, which encouraged people to invest in the newly privatised British Gas.
When we see big shifts in the stock markets there can also be fluctuations in the value of currencies and exchange rates.
As a result, prices could go up, but could also go down.
Upheaval to economies across the world, to oil prices and so on, have a big impact on what we pay at home for goods and services, so there are lots of factors in play.

title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
summary: A post-Brexit deal on food standards has raised questions over the future naming of the classic British snack.
body:
The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.
The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.
Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.
But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.
Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.
On Thursday, Environment Secretary Angela Eagle told a radio presenter he should "get a life" when he asked about the potential impact of the new rules on snacks, such as smoky bacon crisps.
But it highlights the political dangers for the government of realigning with regulations that British politicians have not been able to shape, with the Conservatives and Reform UK keen to pounce on cases showing Britain to be a "rule taker" from Brussels.
It is not the first regulatory skirmish over smoky bacon crisps - following previous headlines over how the well-loved British flavour could be affected by an EU decision in 2024 to phase out a number of artificial smoke flavourings.
Now, the flavour name itself has been called into question by a separate EU attempt to restrict how descriptions of meat are used to market food.
Under rules adopted this summer, the EU plans to restrict the use of 31 terms, including bacon, drumstick and steak, to products that contain meat, claiming consumers could be confused by plant-based alternatives using the same names.
The European snack industry is seeking clarity on how the rules, which will also cover terms such as pork, chicken and beef, would apply to meat-flavoured crisps, including those flavoured without the use of any meat extracts.
The UK government has said it expects the new regulations to be in scope of its proposed food standards deal.
This means they would also apply to companies marketing their products in Britain, which is among the biggest consumers of crisps in Europe,according to analysts Euromonitor.,external
It has raised the prospect that crisps with names such as smoky bacon and roast chicken could have to be relabelled to be sold in British shops, although much remains unclear about how the rules will apply in practice.
The new EU rules, which will not come into force until after August 2029, will allow the European Commission to create exemptions for meaty names with an established long-term use to describe other types of food product.
The Brussels-based body is yet to set out how it plans to use this power, or what it means for snacks.
A group of conservative German MEPs are also seeking a specific carve-out for meat names in snacks and sauces inseparate legislation,externalcurrently making its way through the European Parliament.
The Food and Drink Federation, which represents British crispmakers including Walkers and KP Snacks, has been supportive of the government's bid to reach a food deal due to its potential to reduce trade barriers with Europe.
But it has highlighted the new rules as an example of where it wants the government to work with industry to ensure UK interests are reflected in EU decision making.
"Meat protections are an example of a new EU rule that UK businesses will need to comply with, but which the UK was not involved in developing," added the body's chief scientific officer Kate Halliwell.
The Potato Processors' Association, which also represents a number of major snackmakers, said it was monitoring the situation closely and wanted to see clarification of how the rules could affect its members.
Vanessa Richardson, its deputy director general, said her association supported moves to reduce "unnecessary barriers" in the trade of food products.
But she added it was important that the government's deal is implemented in a way that "avoids unintended consequences for established product descriptions which consumers clearly understand as referring to a flavour".
The Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) says it stands ready to help British snack businesses prepare for the impact of the new EU rules.
It is not yet clear what a British version of the rules would look like, or whether they would need to apply from 2029 alongside the new European regulations.

title: Parliament restoration delays 'frustrating', says Commons Speaker
summary: Sir Lindsay Hoyle urges action after a committee warns it is "crunch time" for the ailing building.
body:
The Speaker of the House of Commons has expressed "frustration" with the lack of progress on restoration to protect the Palace of Westminster.
Sir Lindsay Hoyle told the BBC the current process for approving essential renovations to Parliament amounted to "putting ourselves in handcuffs", and said more time was spent "doing surveys" than getting repairs under way.
The Commons public accounts committee this week warned it was "crunch time" for the ailing building's restoration, which could cost up to £40bn and take 61 years.
It said every additional year of delay cost taxpayers £420m, while its chairman warned the Palacecould be left vulnerable to a devastating firelike that which engulfed the Notre Dame.
Sir Lindsay said his "biggest frustration" with the Victorian building's restoration was that "we're not getting on with the work".
"We spend more time doing surveys," he toldBBC Radio 4's The Week in Westminster. "Instead of doing surveys, why don't we start repairing the building?"
The Speaker criticised current legislation which means the main renovations cannot begin until Parliament has approved the entire project's scope and funding.
"It's very frustrating when the Act of Parliament prevents you carrying out the major repairs that you need to. Talk about putting ourselves in handcuffs."
He added: "What we have to do is renovate and repair the problems areas."
More asbestos found in Parliament, as MPs urged to get on with revamp
Parliament revamp could cost £40bn and take 61 years
Sir Lindsay also questioned why a fire-suppressing mist system had not yet been introduced throughout the building, even though he has called for it for years.
"The major part and the most historic parts of the building haven't got it, and that's what we need."
Asked about reports that Parliament might be given an opportunity to vote on the way forward before the end of 2026, Sir Lindsay said that was a matter for government business managers.
"Who knows when it's going to come forward? Let's see what the House decides," he said.
Much of the 19th-Century building's network of wires and pipes dates back to the 1940s - and some to the Victorian era - according to areport,externalwhich warned of an "impending crisis" a decade ago. Fire safety issues and high levels of asbestos have also been identified.
The BBC understands government whips have discussed holding a debate and vote by the new year, but no date has been scheduled.
This would decide whether to proceed with up to £3bn of initial works and narrow down four current options, ahead of a final decision by 2030.
One proposed option would see MPs and peers move out of the site for up to 24 years from 2032, costing up to £15.6bn.
Another involves moving only the House of Lords out of the building, costing £39bn and taking 61 years.
The chairman of the body in charge of refurbishing Parliamentdefended the potential costs earlier this year, telling the BBC: "We're already spending £150m a year trying to keep the thing standing."

title: PM tells firms to publish salaries in job adverts ahead of new law
summary: The government argues the change will help jobseekers and could help to prevent pay discrimination.
body:
Andy Burnham says it isn't fair if an employer 'holds all the cards'
Businesses should publish salaries in job adverts now, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is telling firms, rather than wait for a new law to come in that will force them to do so.
The government is planning to make pay details compulsory in adverts, with legislation on the issue being brought forward "as soon as possible".
It argues the change will help jobseekers, particularly those applying for their first job, and could help prevent pay discrimination. However, one industry group said setting pay was a complex process and regulating adverts was not always suitable.
It comes a week after the UK's equality watchdog saidemployees should legally be able to find out what their colleagues are earning.
Burnham said the current system felt "weighted against the applicant" and the changes were aimed at "tilting the scales back".
"It can be quite soul destroying for young people these days, applying for jobs when the salary is not listed but sometimes they're not getting a reply," he told the BBC.
The prime minister added that publishing salaries in adverts was also important for closing the gender pay gap.
He was also challenged over whether MPs should be disclosing salaries when advertising for staff in their offices.
A number of politiciansare currently advertising for roles without giving an expected salary.,external
Burnham said: "It would apply completely to them too and the call I'm making today is, before the law changes do it voluntarily because it's the right thing to do."
The Cabinet Office launched a consultation into pay and reducing discrimination in the summer, and the government said there had been "overwhelming support" for greater transparency, with 94% of respondents backing the move.
"Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Burnham said.
The government said the move was part of attempts to reduce the nearly one million young people not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - ahead of the final report of the Milburn Review into youth inactivity, which is due in the coming weeks.
Publishing salary details upfront could "expose unjustified differences in pay, give workers greater confidence to challenge discrimination and prevent disagreements over pay escalating into disputes".
The proposals are similar tomeasures being introduced in the European Union.,external
Employers in Europe will have to disclose the initial pay or range for new roles, which must either be included in a published job advert or shared before an interview.
According to data from UK jobs website Adzuna,external, 51% of the adverts on its site in September had salary information, but the proportion has been falling in recent years.
Adzuna co-founder Andrew Hunter said being open about pay "should be the norm, not the exception".
He added that employers who put a salary on a job advert "attract more applicants, and better-suited ones".
Previous research from the CIPD,external, an industry body for human resources managers, has indicated that the public sector and charities are more likely to reveal pay information that private firms, while pay ranges were more common than specific salaries.
But it found not all employers were "fully transparent", with pay ranges sometimes wider than £10,000.
CIPD chief executive Neil Carberry said that while, in principle, giving salary details was "a good thing", in practice it was "more complicated".
"There isn't always a single fixed figure, and employers will want to set pay based on a candidate's skills, experience and potential."
Carberry added the process was complex, saying that drafting job adverts is "best left to good employer practice rather than government regulation".
The government has said it will set out further details on what information will be required and how the legislation will be enforced "in due course".
Conservative shadow business secretary Julia Lopez said: "At a time when employers are finding it harder and harder to take on staff, Labour have decided to make their lives even more difficult.
"It should be up to businesses to decide what information they advertise about job openings, and to decide how to attract the best applicants.
"As long as they are not being dishonest, misleading or discriminatory, it should not be a matter for the government."
Last week, the Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), said publishing salaries in job adverts would be a "positive step".
It also said bosses should be required to respond to questionnaires about colleagues' pay to cut pay discrimination.
At present, employers do not have to respond to employee requests for salary information about their co-workers.
The EHRC also said employers should be prevented from asking about current salary when offering a job to stop a history of discrimination from continuing.
Employers in the UK are currently allowed to ask you how much you get paid in your current role, butapplicants are under no obligation to tell them.

title: Burnham responds to BBC question over Labour's past links to Brand
summary: The prime minister says that Labour politicians courting the comedian a decade ago had not been aware of his crimes.
body:
In 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when Brand was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said Russell Brand has rightly been held to account for his "horrific" crimes and sought to explain Labour's previous association with the comedian.
Some within the Labour Party attempted to court Brand's support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him - and in 2014 Burnham posted a supportive message on social media when the comedian was facing media criticism about his housing arrangements.
Asked about the 2014 tweet on Friday, Burnham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."
Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault on Thursday.
In 2014, Brand was writing regular opinion pieces for newspapers and appearing on political discussion programmes, including the BBC's Question Time.
His anti-establishment and left-wing views had also gained him a following on social media.
The same year, Burnham, then the shadow health secretary, posted on Twitter in support of Brand following allegations about the comedian's housing arrangements.
It is not clear what Burnham had been referring to in his 2014 tweet, but the previous day, The Sun claimed Brand had paid rent at a property owned by a landlord in a tax haven, while at the same time campaigning against tax avoidance.
Brand threatened to sue the newspaper and said he would give the money to victims of the Hillsborough disaster, a group Burnham has long campaigned for.
At the time, Burnham said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".
Asked about that social media post on Friday, Burnham told the BBC "all I can say is I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing or what he went on to do".
The PM added: "His [Brand's] crimes are horrific, he's rightly been held to account, justice for the victims and that is the right course that's been taken here.
"It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life, but what is important is that where there is wrongdoing it is exposed."
The prime minister added: "Credit to the victims, huge credit, the courage that it's taken, but also the journalists who've exposed this."
Ed Miliband, then the Labour leader, was interviewed by Brand in the run-up to the 2015 general election.
Brand, who had previously dismissed the idea of voting, backed Labour following the interview, saying Miliband had convinced him that "this bloke will listen to us".
Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, has previouslysaid he regrets being interviewed by Brand.
On Friday, a spokesman for Miliband told the BBC: "These are horrific crimes that Russell Brand has been found guilty of and Ed's profound sympathy is with the victims.
"As he said in 2023, 'of course, knowing what I know now - and I was not aware of these allegations at the time about Russell Brand - I wouldn't have done that interview and I regret doing it'."
Brand was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault.
During a four-week trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.
The 51-year-old was refused bail and will spend the weekend in custody before he is due to return to court on Monday for sentencing.

title: Policing needs reform to cope with modern criminals, Met Police chief warns
summary: The Met Police chief used a speech to argue that the current policing system in England and Wales is "heading for failure" without urgent change.
body:
Watch: 'Degradation of policing' by not reforming force, says Met chief
The police system in England and Wales cannot cope against sophisticated modern criminals without urgent reform, the head of the Metropolitan Police has said.
In a speech on Friday, Sir Mark Rowley argued the system was "heading for failure" without change.
He is proposing eight to 10 regional police forces, supported by hundreds of local policing commands and a new national force, in what would be the biggest overhaul of policing since the 1960s.
The changes would replace the 43-force structure with three tiers: local teams dealing with neighbourhood issues, regional forces sharing specialist resources and a National Police Service tackling the most serious crimes.
In January it seemed that the many senior police officers were in favour of creating a National Police Service, and that organising into much larger regional forces had won the argument.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmoodproduced a white paperthat aligned with their ideas and asked the former Metropolitan Police Commissioner Lord Hogan-Howe to look at what the force boundaries might be.
But everything changed in July when Andy Burnham became prime minister. So far, Burnham has not spoken publicly about the plans, and the police chiefs are nervous that they may not have his backing. That may be why they have come out so strongly today, warning of the potentially apocalyptic effect of doing nothing.
As well as pushing hard for large regional forces, they are also making an argument about money which is familiarfrom the defence funding argument.
Sir Mark also pointed out that police funding in England and Wales has fallen from 0.9% of GDP to 0.7%. Implicit in that is that while the slice of the cake being allocated to defending the country is growing, the slice being allocated to defending people's communities and their homes is getting smaller.
Labour wants to shake up the police - but will that solve 'everyday crime epidemic'?
Number of police forces to be cut in major shake-up
Court system under massive strain, warns Met chief
In his speech, Sir Mark saidorganised crime groups, fraud networks, cyber-criminals and those involved in online child abuse increasingly operate across regional and international borders, while police forces remain organised around local areas.
"The victim remains local but increasingly the threat does not," he said citing the example of children who are "groomed by predators on another continent".
He argued that the current system is struggling to keep pace with these threats, saying: "We have 43 overstretched forces trying to do too much, with too little."
Merging forces would reduce duplication and could free up thousands of roles to be redirected towards front line policing, he believes.
Speaking on BBC Breakfast prior to his speech, Sir Mark said crime had changed a lot over the years but the police was largely organised how it was 60 years ago.
"Obviously the world's moved on a long way in that time."
His proposals follow a consultation launched by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood in January. This included plans for a National Police Service to tackle the most complex crimes and a possible merger of the 43 forces into fewer, larger forces.
However some rural police and crime commissioners have described the plans as "political manoeuvring" by larger forces to "load the dice in their favour".
Dorset Police and Crime Commissioner David Sidwick reiterated his strong opposition to proposals to merge the forces.
"My concern is simple. If funding is diverted away from frontline services in Dorset to establish new national structures, local communities could end up receiving less rather than more."
In addition, Kent's Conservative police and crime commissioner Matthew Scott said: "[Sir Mark believes] policing should suffer a decade of disruption, that local policing services should be cut back and made more remote, and that this can all be done without ever asking the public what they want from their local police force."
The Association of Police and Crime Commissioners (APCC) has also questioned whether merging forces is the best way to improve policing.
It said: "The case for modernisation and a National Police Service is clear. The case for reducing 43 forces to nine regional 'mega-forces' is not."
Outgoing Cheshire Chief Constable Mark Roberts also said a future policing model needs to be built in a way that retains the places that already work well so that they do not "get subsumed" and end up "scrabbling to try and get resource from some of the metropolitan areas"
"Bigger isn't always better - we see some high performing big forces, we see some poorer performing big forces.
"The aim is to raise everyone at least to the minimum standard of the best," Roberts said after Rowley's speech.
Asked on Breakfast what would happen if the reforms were not put in place, Sir Mark said: "the risk is failure".
"Failure means solving fewer crimes, less local presence, when you get exceptional incidents like a certain outbreak of disorder like we saw in Hampshire."
In September police clashed withanti-migrant protesters in Portsmouthwhen 120 migrants arrived in a single dinghy.
"Standing still looks like a degradation of policing day by day, struggling even more as criminals outpace policing because we're not organised to meet it," Sir Mark added.
A Home Office spokesperson defended the plans, saying: "Our current model of policing has not changed since the 1960s and is no longer fit for purpose."
Sir Mark has also highlighted the financial pressures facing policing, saying that spending on policing had fallen from about 0.9% of GDP to 0.7% since 2010, which he said was as "a big hit".
"We do need investment as well, but if you threw loads of money at the current system it's still not going to fix the fundamental problem, it's not designed to meet today's challenges," he told the BBC.
"Throwing money at the current system isn't going to work."
Sir Mark said in his speech that years of underinvestment hasleft forces relying on ageing technology, and officers are increasingly diverted from neighbourhood policing to deal with other demands, including mental health and social care.
He also pointedto falling police performance, saying positive outcomes nationally are now less than half the level they were 12 years ago, while public confidence has fallen by 9%.

title: Why smoky bacon crisps threaten to reignite rows over EU rules
summary: A post-Brexit deal on food standards has raised questions over the future naming of the classic British snack.
body:
The naming of smoky bacon-flavoured crisps has become the latest political headache to emerge from the government's bid for closer ties with the EU.
The government is negotiating a deal on food standards in a bid to cut costs for British companies trading with Europe.
Labour ministers have been keen to talk up the potential economic benefits of the agreement, which could be announced at a summit later this month.
But the deal's requirement for Britain to adopt EU food rules in a wide range of areas has threatened to reignite sovereignty debates from the Brexit era.
Labour ministers have been keen to sidestep talking about the impact of alignment in particular sectors, instead stressing the overall economic boost it expects the food deal to bring.
On Thursday, Environment Secretary Angela Eagle told a radio presenter he should "get a life" when he asked about the potential impact of the new rules on snacks, such as smoky bacon crisps.
But it highlights the political dangers for the government of realigning with regulations that British politicians have not been able to shape, with the Conservatives and Reform UK keen to pounce on cases showing Britain to be a "rule taker" from Brussels.
It is not the first regulatory skirmish over smoky bacon crisps - following previous headlines over how the well-loved British flavour could be affected by an EU decision in 2024 to phase out a number of artificial smoke flavourings.
Now, the flavour name itself has been called into question by a separate EU attempt to restrict how descriptions of meat are used to market food.
Under rules adopted this summer, the EU plans to restrict the use of 31 terms, including bacon, drumstick and steak, to products that contain meat, claiming consumers could be confused by plant-based alternatives using the same names.
The European snack industry is seeking clarity on how the rules, which will also cover terms such as pork, chicken and beef, would apply to meat-flavoured crisps, including those flavoured without the use of any meat extracts.
The UK government has said it expects the new regulations to be in scope of its proposed food standards deal.
This means they would also apply to companies marketing their products in Britain, which is among the biggest consumers of crisps in Europe,according to analysts Euromonitor.,external
It has raised the prospect that crisps with names such as smoky bacon and roast chicken could have to be relabelled to be sold in British shops, although much remains unclear about how the rules will apply in practice.
The new EU rules, which will not come into force until after August 2029, will allow the European Commission to create exemptions for meaty names with an established long-term use to describe other types of food product.
The Brussels-based body is yet to set out how it plans to use this power, or what it means for snacks.
A group of conservative German MEPs are also seeking a specific carve-out for meat names in snacks and sauces inseparate legislation,externalcurrently making its way through the European Parliament.
The Food and Drink Federation, which represents British crispmakers including Walkers and KP Snacks, has been supportive of the government's bid to reach a food deal due to its potential to reduce trade barriers with Europe.
But it has highlighted the new rules as an example of where it wants the government to work with industry to ensure UK interests are reflected in EU decision making.
"Meat protections are an example of a new EU rule that UK businesses will need to comply with, but which the UK was not involved in developing," added the body's chief scientific officer Kate Halliwell.
The Potato Processors' Association, which also represents a number of major snackmakers, said it was monitoring the situation closely and wanted to see clarification of how the rules could affect its members.
Vanessa Richardson, its deputy director general, said her association supported moves to reduce "unnecessary barriers" in the trade of food products.
But she added it was important that the government's deal is implemented in a way that "avoids unintended consequences for established product descriptions which consumers clearly understand as referring to a flavour".
The Department for Environment, Food & Rural Affairs (Defra) says it stands ready to help British snack businesses prepare for the impact of the new EU rules.
It is not yet clear what a British version of the rules would look like, or whether they would need to apply from 2029 alongside the new European regulations.
